extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers and informed readers interested in analytic number theory and the Riemann zeta function
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of conjectures, theorems, explicit bounds, numerical methods and analogues concerning the location and distribution of zeros of the Riemann zeta function and related L‑functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized Riemann hypothesis (Dirichlet L-functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extends the Riemann hypothesis to all Dirichlet L‑functions: the non-trivial zeros of these global L‑functions are expected to have real part 1/2. In particular it implies that Siegel zeros (zeros between 1/2 and 1) do not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States scope (Dirichlet L‑functions), consequence (no Siegel zeros). Presents as the most common generalization of RH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended Riemann hypothesis (Dedekind zeta functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extends the Riemann hypothesis to all Dedekind zeta functions of algebraic number fields. For abelian extensions of Q the Dedekind zeta factors as products of Dirichlet L‑functions, so this version implies the generalized RH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains implication relations between versions (Dedekind RH ⇒ Dirichlet RH in appropriate cases) and notes considerations about poles (only possible pole at s=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann hypothesis for Hecke L‑functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extends RH to L‑functions of Hecke characters of number fields; since Dirichlet L‑functions are special cases, this version implies the generalized RH for Dirichlet L‑functions and, via factorization, the Dedekind version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes logical implications between Hecke, Dirichlet and Dedekind versions and notes the pole locations (Hecke L‑functions only possible pole at 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand Riemann hypothesis (Automorphic L‑functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension of RH to all automorphic L‑functions (e.g. Mellin transforms of Hecke eigenforms); conjecturally the most general form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places this as one of the most general extensions; relates expectation that Selberg class = automorphic L‑functions and mentions connection to Langlands program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann hypothesis for the Selberg class
rubrics_metrics.description: Poses RH for functions in the Selberg class—functions satisfying certain (conjectural) axioms which many zeta/L‑functions obey—predicting their nontrivial zeros lie on the central line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that equality of Selberg class and automorphic L‑functions is expected but open; presents this as an alternative general formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized RH for arithmetic zeta functions of schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming functional equation and meromorphic continuation, the generalized RH for an L‑factor of an n‑dimensional regular connected equidimensional arithmetic scheme states zeros with Re(s) in (0,n) lie on the central line; for the arithmetic zeta function its zeros inside the critical strip lie on vertical lines Re(s)=1/2,3/2,...,n−1/2 and its poles on Re(s)=1,2,...,n−1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the precise vertical lines where zeros/poles are expected, notes it's known in positive characteristic (Deligne) but unknown in characteristic zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero‑free regions (explicit inequalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit regions in the complex plane where zeros cannot occur, typically of the form σ ≥ 1 − C / f(|t|) for various functions f. The page lists several explicit recent inequalities (Mossinghoff, Trudgian & Yang 2022) giving four improved zero‑free regions with stated ranges of |t|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete forms (e.g. σ ≥ 1 − 1/(5.558691 log|t|), σ ≥ 1 − 1/(55.241 (log|t|)^{2/3}(log log|t|)^{1/3}), etc.), specifies ranges of |t| where each bound applies and notes improvements and limitations ('sufficiently large' caveat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeros on the critical line — provable proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Results establishing how many zeros lie exactly on the critical line Re(s)=1/2: Hardy (infinitely many), Selberg (positive proportion), Levinson (≥1/3), Conrey (≥2/5), and Pratt/Robles/Zaharescu/Zeindler (≥5/12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents these as successive improvements in lower bounds for the proportion of zeros on the critical line, and notes the techniques (relations to zeros of derivatives, mollifiers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero density estimates / Bohr–Landau result
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that bound the number of zeros with real part ≥1/2+ε and |Im| ≤ T; in particular Bohr & Landau showed the number is O(T), implying almost all zeros lie within any fixed small distance ε of the critical line because the total number of zeros is Θ(T log T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes these as 'zero density estimates' (Ivić) giving more precise bounds; used to show that most nontrivial zeros are close to the line even absent RH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture that the normalized pair correlation of zeros of ζ(1/2+it) matches that of eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices (GUE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes motivation (statistical properties similarity), Odlyzko's numerical evidence supporting it, and consequences such as implications about simplicity of zeros (Montgomery showed assuming RH at least 2/3 of zeros are simple).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert–Pólya conjecture / operator approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggests RH would follow from exhibiting a self‑adjoint operator whose eigenvalues correspond (via 1/2 + i·eigenvalue) to zeros of ζ(s); analogies cited include zeros as eigenvalues for Selberg zeta, Frobenius action in finite fields, and p‑adic situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the idea, supporting analogies, and specific physics‑inspired conjectures (e.g. Berry–Keating quantization of H = xp), plus caveats about practical usefulness (e.g. operator involving inverse potential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical verification methodology (Z function and Turing's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify RH up to height T: find sign changes of Hardy's Z(t) (so locate zeros on the critical line), and use Turing's method to compute the total number of zeros in the region and confirm it matches the number found on the line. This verification requires that all zeros in the region are simple and on the critical line to use the checking methods reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains decomposition ζ(1/2+it)=Z(t)e^{-iθ(t)}, locating Gram points, checking sign changes of Z, and the role of Turing's method to ensure no off‑line zeros; notes computational prerequisites (simplicity of zeros) and that this procedure can, in principle, verify RH up to any T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gram's law and Rosser's rule (Gram points behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical/heuristic statements: Gram's law — usually exactly one zero between consecutive Gram points; refinements: signs of (−1)^n Z(g_n) usually positive. Rosser's rule: Gram blocks (intervals bounded by two good Gram points with bad Gram points inside) often contain the expected number of zeros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes failures: Gram's law and Rosser's rule fail infinitely often and Trudgian (2011) showed they fail in positive proportion; gives definition of good/bad Gram points and Gram blocks and examples of first failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Siegel formula and computational complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Riemann–Siegel formula is an efficient method for computing ζ(s) on the critical line; using it takes about O(T^{3/2+ε}) steps to check zeros up to height T, compared with O(T^{2+ε}) for direct Euler–Maclaurin summation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains computational advantage and historical shift to using Riemann–Siegel for large zero computations; references to large scale computations (Titchmarsh, Odlyzko, Gourdon, Platt & Trudgian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit bound on N(T) (Trudgian 2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit bound controlling the error in the zero counting function N(T): |N(T) − (T/(2π)) log(T/(2πe))| ≤ 0.112 log T + 0.278 log log T + 3.385 + 0.2/T for T > e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit quantitative control on the deviation of N(T) from its main term; useful in rigorous computations and error estimates when counting zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turán's criterion and its limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Turán showed that if finite Dirichlet series ∑_{n=1}^N n^{-s} have no zeros for Re(s)>1 then a certain sum T(x)=∑_{n≤x} λ(n)/n ≥ 0 for x>0, which would imply RH. However Haselgrove showed T(x) is negative infinitely often, and Montgomery showed finite series have zeros beyond the stated bound, so Turán's result is vacuous for proving RH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the logical connection Turán proposed, and why later results (Haselgrove, Montgomery) render the approach unable to prove RH; includes explicit counterexamples and commentary on vacuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lehmer's phenomenon (nearby zeros causing numerical difficulty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where two zeros are unusually close (e.g. Lehmer's pair), making it difficult to detect sign changes between them numerically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights practical numerical issue when zeros are very close (first occurs around imaginary parts ~7005), noting implications for zero‑finding algorithms that rely on sign changes.
